scenes.question: A structured-output reply passed schema validation. What do you know?
options: Every value in it is true

scenes.explain: Validation guarantees shape, not truth. Check meaning in code where you can, like the grounding check.

items.text: Schemas: only fields you use, with constraints and descriptions
The API guarantees shape; the SDK validates limits
Cut off, invalid, refused: one clear error each

captions.text: Programs need data, not prose.
In Module 2 you asked for a quiz as structured output.
Now we go deeper: how to design a schema, what structured outputs guarantee, what
they don't, and how to handle every kind of parsing failure with one clear error.
You'll design Pydantic schemas with useful constraints.
Know what structured outputs guarantee, and what they don't.
Handle replies that are cut off, invalid, refused, or invented.
And check meaning in code, not just shape.
A schema is a contract between the model and your code.
The candidate profile has a name, years of experience, a list of skills, and recent
roles.
Every field is something code will actually use.
Field adds constraints.
Years of experience must be between zero and sixty.
A negative number is a bug, and we want to catch it.
A description tells the model what belongs in a field.
Here: technical skills the resume names, as written.
Job requirements split skills into must have and nice to have.
That split is what makes the comparison meaningful.
And suggestions are a summary plus one piece of advice per skill.
Notice there's no reasoning field.
Ask only for what you'll use.
Current models reason before they answer anyway.
With structured outputs, the API constrains the reply to your schema.
You get valid JSON, with your fields and your types.
Some constraints, like minimum and maximum values, can't be enforced during
generation.
The SDK moves them into the field description, and validates them with Pydantic when
the reply arrives.
If one fails, you get a validation error.
And what's never guaranteed is truth.
A perfectly valid reply can still contain a wrong value, or a skill the resume never
mentions.
Let's see what Pydantic reports for four replies.
This needs no model at all: it's the same validation the SDK runs.
A good reply becomes an object.
A negative number of years fails greater than or equal.
A missing field is reported as missing.
And a reply cut off in the middle isn't JSON at all: json invalid.
Every model call in the project goes through this one method.
It calls parse with the schema as output format, the system prompt, the rendered
template, and an effort level.
If validation fails, we look at the first error.
Invalid JSON almost always means the reply was cut off by max tokens, so we say
that.
Any other validation error names the field and the problem, in one line.
Then we record the call: which prompt, its fingerprint, tokens, and cost.
And we check the stop reason: a refusal, or a reply that was cut off, never gets
returned as if it were complete.
Structured output checks the shape.
Code can check meaning too.
Mentions asks: does the resume text actually name this skill, or one of its aliases?
Grounded splits the extracted skills into those the resume names, and those it
doesn't.
The analyzer keeps the first list, drops the second, and tells you what it dropped.
The project's fake API can misbehave on purpose, so we can watch each failure path.
A reply with negative years becomes one clear error that names the field.
A reply cut off mid-JSON: not complete JSON, cut off.
And when the reply invents a skill, here COBOL, the grounding check drops it and
tells us.
Quick check.
A structured output reply passed validation.
What do you actually know?
That it has the right fields and types.
Shape, not truth.
Where you can, check meaning in code.
A schema holds only the fields you use, with constraints and descriptions.
The API guarantees the shape, and the SDK validates the limits.
Cut-off, invalid, and refused replies each become one clear error.
And code checks meaning, like grounding every skill in the resume.
